answers.label: Benefits and challenges of consequential methods
answers.text:
The proposal to discuss consequential electricity-sector emissions impact as a separate metric from attributional accounting, only counting towards mitigation of the scope 2 emissions inventory when the underlying procurement happens to meet the proposed hourly- and location-matching quality criteria for market-based instruments, is a detrimental design flaw. Emissions accounting per the GHG Protocol Scope 2 Standard has been successful thus far because enterprises around the world have chosen to adopt it as their standardized methodology, as it measured legitimacy alongside feasibility. The current proposal, wherein causation of new renewable energy is relegated to a separate consequential accounting rather than integral to attributional accounting itself, will not provide any motivational value to companies to leverage this voluntary standard and, more importantly, the voluntary procurement mechanism derived from the GHGP standards.

We have advised over 100 global corporations on a multi-year basis over the last 15+ years; each of those corporations were motivated towards driving an impactful renewable energy strategy, despite having cheaper and logistically easier options on the open unbundled EAC market, primarily by the fact that the consequential accounting currently implicit in the market-based method was a viable method of scope 2 emissions reduction. Removing and reallocating this primary incentive to a separate consequential accounting approach would obviate the reason all of our clients have chosen the “hard right” of causing new clean energy generation through long-term forward PPAs” over the “easy wrong” of buying unbundled EACs from long-existing projects in the spot market, that are coincidentally matched 24/7 with their demand.

If consequential impact were integrated into attribution accounting as a key quality criterion for market-based instruments whenever feasible, GHGP would have the unique opportunity to not only enhance momentum towards bringing new renewable energy onto the grid but also clarify how an off-site renewable energy procurement can be validated as causing new renewable energy capacity. SR Inc has long advocated for such criteria to be made clear through the establishment of a “purchaser-caused” tag when a procurement meets specific requirements, which we will articulate further in questions 26 & 27 of this survey. This is critical because companies marketing non-causative EACs as additional undermine the credibility of the EAC market, which cannot be afforded.

Undermining the Scope 2 emissions accounting incentive to serve as the proximate cause of new clean energy capacity is a mistake, especially if it is done to advance a specious “use claim” through a pseudo “deliverability” for a pseudo “inventory,” as is currently proposed by the hourly- and location-matching requirements. The current Scope 2 market-based method accounting is a consequential accounting that rightly recognizes procurement of clean energy generation, not consumption, and GHGP can further enhance this standard to legitimize the work of all the companies that have contributed to nearly 140 GW of new renewables on the US grid, momentum which must continue to reduce the most catastrophic effects of human-caused climate breakdown.

answers.label: Secondary effects to consider, and how
answers.text:
The human health impacts of renewable energy should be considered including, but not limited to, avoided pollution, public health, ecosystem and economic impacts. This analysis can include (1) Global perspective: Net benefits analysis integrating both pollution increases from infrastructure manufacturing and pollution decreases due to operation of the project; (2) Operational perspective: Avoided local and global air pollutants and resource use due to operation of the project; (3) Local perspective: Avoided local air pollutants and resource use in and around the project area due to operation of the project. In its first year of operation, the 1 GW portfolio of renewable energy capacity that SR Inc Member-Clients enabled through aggregated procurements for utility-scale renewable energy generated:

1. $925M in health systems cost savings
2. 1,600,000 MT CO2 emissions avoided
3. 3,694 disability-adjusted human life years saved
4. 7 distinct species saved.

These figures come from Quantum Energy’s TotalView Energy Platform, which considers the three aforementioned perspectives and uses metrics related to emissions to air, emissions to water, emissions to soil, and resource use to quantify the pubic health, ecosystem, and economic impacts of not only the addition of new renewable energy capacity to the grid but the displacement of fossil fuel infrastructure from the grid. These metrics are critical secondary effects of the addition of new renewable energy capacity to the grid and should be considered in impact criteria.

answers.label: Requiredness of the financial analysis test
Requiredness of the common practice test
Why selected tests should be included
answers.text:
1. Timing test: For a project to be considered “additional,” the timing test is necessary to require a pre-financing contractual commitment to pay for the bundled new renewable energy generating capacity & EACs produced by the project. If the project is already financed, a buyer cannot claim to have “caused” new renewable energy capacity as the project would have come online without the financial backing brought in by the buyer. The contractual agreement should also come before construction, though financing almost always comes before construction. However, “under construction” should be defined as the actual physical construction of the project, after FNTP is achieved, not “under construction” by current U.S. tax incentive rules. It is unimportant whether the project was already planned, as many planned projects do not eventuate into operating plants.
2. Barrier test: Similarly to the above, and particularly if the timing test only applies to situations where the project is pre-planning or pre-construction, the barrier test should be used to demonstrate that lack of financing was a barrier to the project’s execution, and the contract for EACs along with the investment grade credit rating, or posted Letter of Credit, of the buyer(s) was the catalyst to overcome that barrier. The contractual commitment to pay for the RECs bundled with the new generation capacity must happen before the project is financed.
3. Contractual/tenor test: For a project to be considered additional, the EAC procurement term must be at least 10 years (as the market has empirically demonstrated), and the contract must bundle the cost of energy with the cost of the EACs. Long-term contracts are necessary to help demonstrate that buyers provided the financial certainty needed for financing, so the length of the term is critical in assuring that the project gets built, and the developer is guaranteed a long-term offtaker for the EACS in advance. The bundling of the EACs and the cost of energy is also necessary for ensuring that the buyer takes on the downside risk which enables potential financers to move forward with the project.

answers.label: Context on test feasibility
answers.text:
a. In the current regulatory environment, a regulatory test is infeasible because in-practice laws require a certain percentage of energy in a given region to be generated from renewables; however, whether a specific project was necessary to hit that percentage would be impossible to prove. Also, even if renewable energy generation were required because of a regulatory requirement like BEUDO or BERDO, that does not negate the fact that new capacity is still contributing to making the grid greener, which is the ultimate goal. So, even if this test were feasible, it would not be desirable.
b. There are several pieces of data one could point to in order to prove that the contract for the EACs generated by a project came before financing was secured by the developer. 1) The date of the signed contract should be earlier than the date of “Final Notice to Proceed,” or FNTP. FNTP must be given in order for the financer to proceed with delivering the financing to the developer. 2) One could source anecdotal responses from developers describing their process for obtaining financing, and any notice they received from financers about the level of downside risk they would have to mitigate through long-term EAC contracts in order to proceed with financing.
c. A financial analysis test would be infeasible because determining a universal threshold level of financial attractiveness that is acceptable to a wide range of developers and financing institutional funds (which demonstrate an array of risk/return thresholds for investing funds), as well across different markets and transaction types would be impossible.
d. Depending on the barrier being evaluated this test may or may not be feasible, and this is also dependent on who is trying to claim additionality. If a solar panel manufacturer wanted to claim additionality on a project because it wouldn’t have been possible without the supply of solar panels, this would be a dubious claim. However, in the case that lack of financing was the barrier to preventing a project from moving forward, and the long-term contract for EACs was the incentive to overcome it, this can be proved through the same methods described for the timing test.
e. While the common practice test is theoretically feasible to prove, it is not practically desirable. Even if many solar projects are already implemented in a given region, each one of them certainly took significant effort to bring into operation, which justifies the tag of additionality. Second, as EACs are used to claim renewable energy, and the EAC is itself an incentive, there are very few examples today of renewable energy projects, let alone many in a given region or market, that are entirely without incentives. This criterion might be better evaluated in a market closer to achieving real zero (e.g. Costa Rica). Furthermore, given the current state of the market, the goal of an “additionality” tag is to incentivize adding new renewable energy capacity to the grid. So, even if the solar had achieved cost-parity with non-renewable alternatives without EACs or tax credits, these standards should still consider new solar capacity as “additional.”
f. Depending on the criteria included in the positive list test, it could be feasible to implement, but other tests are more relevant.
g. Performance standard: While the performance standard test might be feasible, it is muddied by the arbitrary nature of a baseline emissions rate or energy efficiency level which have nothing to do with whether a project adds new renewable energy capacity to the grid.
h. Given that nearly all legal contracts have a defined “term,” it would be straightforward to test for tenor of a project. Also, given the clarity necessitated by legal contracts, it should also be easy to prove whether a contract bundles the EACs with the cost of electricity through a fixed price, flat price, or some other pricing structure.
i. A first-of-its-kind test is immaterial in whether a project adds new capacity.

answers.label: Additionality tests missing from the framework
answers.text: Optional project capacity test: The standard could include an optional minimum capacity test that is region-specific, allowing for that amount to be procured individually or in aggregate (e.g. 50MW for U.S. solar). This scale encourages the addition of utility-scale capacity to the grid. The size is included because it helps ensure that the developer couldn’t finance the project on their own, so the other tests should cover this. This could also be the impetus for a different tag, an “additional utility-scale” tag.

answers.label: Claims possible under different test approaches
answers.text:
Not all renewable energy procurements generate equal impact. There is an important distinction to be made between EACs bought from an existing system that a corporate buyer had no influence in causing, EACs bought from a system that a corporate buyer contributed to the financing of, and EACs bought from a system that would not have existed without the role of the corporate buyer in the procurement process.
The first option, unbundled EACs purchased from the spot mark, represent the lowest value option. They are often bought from projects that were developed years earlier. While inexpensive, they do not impact the greening of the grid whatsoever.
The second option, “Contributing EACs,” offer a modest improvement over the above but fall well short of maximal impact. Typically, corporates provide incremental capital to renewable energy projects primarily financed by other sources. They are more expensive, and more impactful, but they still cannot claim to proximately cause new renewable energy deployment to the grid. Attributing the same value to these “Contributing EACs” as one would to “Purchaser-caused EACs” or “Causal EACs,” would threaten market credibility.
The third option, “Purchaser-caused EACs” or “Causal EACs,” represent genuine “additionality.” These procurements directly cause new renewable energy projects to be built by meeting three key criteria:
1. Bundled prefinancing commitment: Procurements that contract to cover the cost of a clean energy project’s development AND its resulting EACs.
2. Sufficient duration: Procurements that commit to a term of ten or more years.
3. Optional - Sufficient volume: Procurements that commit to 40 MW or more of capacity (alone or with others’ simultaneous matching contracts).
When procurements meet these three thresholds, companies demonstrably cause renewable energy capacity that wouldn’t otherwise exist to be added to the grid. This difference matters enormously for the world to achieve its climate goals. The COP28 UAE Consensus identified the tripling of renewable energy deployment by 2030 as essential to avoiding climate catastrophe and achieving this goal necessitates corporate procurement that actually builds new capacity, not just redistributes EACs from existing projects.
Industry consensus surrounding what constitutes causation is clear among experienced corporate buyers, so companies serious about climate impact must be incentivized by the market and the standards they follow to prioritize causation over contribution.
